statement: Transformer VA rating is not the same as watts: power factor is W/VA, and a capacitor-input rectifier draws current in short peaks, so the VA rating must exceed the DC power.
In ESP's 25 V RMS, 0.75 Ohm, 1.44 A DC, 4,700 uF example, the secondary RMS current was 2.71 A and the peak current 6.40 A, giving a power factor of about 0.73.
The RMS secondary current is approximately 1.8 times the DC current for a bridge rectifier, 1.2 times for a full-wave centre-tap, and 1.8 times for a dual supply loaded in common mode.
Half-wave rectification should not be used above a few milliamps because the DC component can saturate a transformer, especially a toroid, at about 20 mA.
Required reservoir capacitance is approximately C = (I_L / delta_V) x k x 1,000 uF, with k = 6 for 120 Hz and k = 7 for 100 Hz ripple.

The formula gives about 3,500 uF per amp for 2 V peak-to-peak ripple at 50 Hz and about 3,000 uF per amp at 60 Hz; ESP recommends a minimum of 2,000 uF per amp DC, which allows about 3 V peak-to-peak.
Doubling the reservoir capacitance halves ripple voltage for a given load current but changes steady-state RMS and peak transformer current very little; it does substantially increase inrush current.
ESP argues that the claim that large reservoir capacitance causes steady-state transformer overheating is a myth; the increase is an inrush transient, not a steady-state current.
Capacitor ripple-current rating must not be exceeded; two 4,700 uF capacitors usually have a higher combined ripple rating and lower ESR than one 10,000 uF capacitor.
A larger transformer has lower winding resistance and better regulation, but it places greater ripple-current stress on the reservoir capacitor.
ESP's 60 VA, 0.75 Ohm, 4,700 uF example had about 16% regulation at 1.61 A DC, compared with about 5% for the same transformer into a resistive load.
Toroidal transformers have much higher inter-winding capacitance than EI transformers and couple more common-mode mains noise; an electrostatic shield or side-by-side windings reduce it.
Transformer flux density is highest at no load, so mechanical noise is greatest at idle and low audio levels.
Toroidal transformers need slow-blow fuses; a toroid of 500 VA or more benefits from soft start; a 100 W/8 Ohm amplifier may need a 3 A slow-blow fuse at 240 V or 6 A at 120 V.
A primary fuse does not protect the amplifier against output overload or shorted speaker leads; secondary DC fuses should always be used.

With transformers of 300 VA or less, inrush is typically limited by primary resistance and mains impedance to about 50 A at 230 V and lasts less than one AC cycle; larger transformers need soft start.
A soft start should limit peak current to 2 to 5 times the normal full-power operating current; for a 2 A maximum at 230 V this means 23 to 58 Ohm.
A switch-mode supply has no transformer primary resistance to limit inrush; ESP measured 80 A peak for a 150 W SMPS and more than 10 A for a 20 W SMPS.

A conventional linear supply is repairable and long-lived, while a switch-mode supply often fails through high-ESR electrolytic capacitors and may be unrepairable once specialised ICs are unavailable.

ESP's minimum transformer VA rules are approximately equal to amplifier power for Class-AB, 4 to 5 times (up to 10 times) for single-ended Class-A, and approximately nominal power for Class-D with adequate regulation.
ESP's reservoir minimums are 4,700 uF per 100 W into 8 Ohm and 10,000 uF per 100 W into 4 Ohm for Class-AB, and 4,700 uF per 10 W into 8 Ohm for Class-A.

ESP's rectifier guidance is a 35 A/400 V bridge for amplifiers of 50 W or more, with current of at least 6 A per 100 W into 8 Ohm or 12 A per 100 W into 4 Ohm, and voltage of at least 200 V for 100 W into 8 Ohm or 100 V for 100 W into 4 Ohm.
ESP recommends a reservoir ripple-current rating of about twice the peak output current for Class-AB, for example 7 A for a 100 W/8 Ohm amplifier, and five times the load current for Class-A.
A capacitance multiplier is a buffered filter, not a literal capacitance multiplier; a two-pole version changes the roll-off from 6 dB/octave to 12 dB/octave.
A 1 kOhm and 1,000 uF filter has a 0.159 Hz corner and attenuates 100 Hz ripple by about 56 dB, reducing 1 V RMS to 1.6 mV.
ESP states that with two 500 Ohm resistors and two 500 uF capacitors the second-order filter is nearly 74 dB down at 100 Hz, and that about 60 dB is easily achieved in practice.
A resistor from the output to ground keeps the output just below the ripple trough; without it the output ripple is more than 30 times greater.
A capacitance multiplier is intolerant of an output short circuit; the series-pass transistors can fail almost instantly, with no safe short-circuit duration.
In ESP's comparison the two-pole multiplier gave 246 mV peak-to-peak ripple versus just over 1 V for a pi filter, but dropped about 2.7 V at 3.6 A and dissipated about 10 W.
A MOSFET capacitance multiplier typically loses at least 4.5 V and has poor transient response because the gate has no rapid discharge path, with the gate staying high for up to 250 ms.
An LDO uses a PNP or P-channel pass device with the output taken from the collector or drain, so it relies on feedback for low output impedance and is not inherently stable.
LDO stability often depends on output-capacitor ESR; a very low-ESR 10 uF ceramic may oscillate, and the TPS76050 example needs at least 100 mOhm for stability.
Adding more output capacitance can make an LDO less stable, not more.
A conventional emitter-follower regulator is stable with almost any output capacitor and ESR, but typically needs about 3 V input-to-output differential.
LDO dropout can be 100 to 200 mV at low current, versus about 3 V for a conventional regulator.
The LM317 has 0.003% of VOUT output noise (75 uV at 2.5 V), while a TPS76425 has a little over 60 uV at 10 mA.
LDO output noise increases with output current and is critical when powering ADCs and DACs, which have much lower supply rejection than op-amps.
High-K ceramic dielectrics lose capacitance with applied voltage, aging and temperature, which can affect LDO stability.
Bypass capacitors on IC supply rails are part of the LDO output capacitance and can cause unforeseen stability problems.
TI's SLYT202 defines PSRR as 20 log (input ripple / output ripple) over a frequency range, commonly 10 Hz to 10 MHz, so a larger positive number means better rejection.
LDO PSRR has three frequency regions: from DC to the bandgap-filter roll-off, from there to the unity-gain frequency, and above unity gain where the output capacitor and parasitics dominate.
Higher load current lowers LDO open-loop gain and therefore low-frequency PSRR, while moving the output pole higher and raising high-frequency PSRR.
When VIN minus VOUT falls below about 1 V the pass FET can enter the triode region, reducing loop gain and PSRR; the required headroom rises with load current.
PSRR is usually better at lower output voltages.
A larger output capacitor with lower ESR typically improves PSRR above the unity-gain frequency, but can reduce it at some frequencies by lowering the unity-gain frequency.
The bandgap reference is a dominant internal PSRR path; it is usually filtered by a large internal resistor and an external capacitor.
Board layout must reduce input-to-output feedthrough parasitics to preserve LDO PSRR.
Dropout voltage is the input-to-output differential at which regulation ceases; in dropout a PMOS pass element behaves as a resistor, so Vdropout = Iout x Ron.
The TPS76733 3.3 V LDO has 350 mV typical dropout at 1 A, so it begins to drop out at about 3.65 V input.
Quiescent current is the difference between input and output current and includes the reference, error amplifier and pass-device base or gate current.
LDO output noise is specified as RMS noise over 10 Hz to 100 kHz with a constant load and ripple-free input; most output noise comes from the internal reference.

LDO stability is specified as a range of compensation series resistance (CSR = ESR + added resistance) versus output current; the TPS763xx example is stable for CSR between 0.2 Ohm and 9 Ohm, the so-called tunnel of death.
A larger output capacitor with low ESR improves PSRR, provided the CSR stability requirement is met.
TI's SLVA079 defines ripple rejection as the ratio of output ripple to input ripple at all frequencies, the reciprocal of the SLYT202 definition; the sign convention must be stated.
The LM317 reference voltage is 1.25 V typical, the output is adjustable from 1.25 V to 37 V, and the current limit is 1.5 A.
The LM317 RMS output noise is 0.003% of VOUT over 10 Hz to 10 kHz.
LM317 ripple rejection is 57 dB typical without C_ADJ and 62 to 64 dB with C_ADJ = 10 uF for the legacy chip; the new chip is 65 dB without and 66 to 80 dB with C_ADJ, at VOUT = 10 V and 120 Hz.
LM317 line regulation is 0.01%/V typical and 0.04%/V maximum at 25 C; load regulation is 25 mV for VOUT up to 5 V or 0.1 to 0.5% of VOUT.
LM317 thermal regulation is 0.04%/W typical for a 20 ms pulse.

A capacitor-input linear supply is not linear: current flows from the transformer only when the AC voltage exceeds the stored capacitor voltage, so the current waveform is highly non-linear and can inject noise into nearby wiring, including speaker cables.

Transformer secondary voltage is specified at full rated current into a resistive load; a 100 VA, 30 V transformer gives about 33.5 V RMS unloaded and about 45 V DC after a bridge, and its DC output can fall from 46 V to 38 V at full load, a regulation worse than 17%.
Mains voltage is nominally 230 V or 120 V with about +/-10% tolerance but is often worse, and the secondary voltage tracks it, so calculated DC voltages are approximate.

A Class-AB amplifier may draw only 20 to 100 mA at idle but many amps when driven, and each supply lead sees half-wave current pulses in sympathy with the programme; the sharp transitions generate magnetic fields.

A Class-A amplifier draws its maximum current continuously, making poor earthing more apparent; transformer leakage flux can also cause buzz, so DC, speaker and signal wiring should be kept away from the transformer.
The LM317 output voltage is VOUT = 1.25 V x (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ x R2, and bypassing the adjustment pin improves ripple rejection.
The LM317 minimum load current is 3.5 mA typical and 10 mA maximum at a 40 V input-to-output differential.
LM317 legacy-chip junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 66.8 C/W in SOT-223, 23.5 C/W in TO-220 (KCS), 37.9 C/W in TO-220 (KCT), and 38.0 C/W in TO-263.

ESP notes that some transformer manufacturers suggest a VA rating of only 0.7 times the maximum amplifier power; this works for most music but does not give a stiff supply, and the DC voltage collapses as more current is drawn.
